title: Why are airplane windows round?
question: Why does every window and opening in an airliner cabin have rounded corners?
answer: A pressurised cabin is loaded on every flight; sharp corners concentrate that stress and grow fatigue cracks, as the 1954 Comet breakups showed, so rounded corners spread the load.
problem: Square openings in a pressurised fuselage pile stress into their corners, and every flight repeats the load until a crack grows.
solution: Rounded windows that spread the stress, plus fatigue testing of whole fuselages and crack stoppers in the skin.
surprise: The Comet's fatal crack began at a small roof antenna opening, not a passenger window; and your window hides a tiny hole that makes the outer pane do the work.
people_rule: People are anonymous representative passengers, crew and engineers. Never a real victim's face, never invented dialogue.

c1.text: On 2 May 1952 BOAC flew the first jet airliner passenger service, a de Havilland Comet from London to Johannesburg with stops on the way.
sources: FlightGlobal, 'How Comet's debut service launched the passenger jet age', https://flightglobal.com/flight-international/how-comets-debut-service-launched-the-passenger-jet-age/148341.article

c2.text: The Comet was designed to cruise at about 40,000 ft (Wikipedia: design cruising altitude 40,000 ft; Engineers Ireland: the Elba flight was climbing to about 36,000 ft).
sources: Engineers Ireland, 'Beyond the limits of imagination: what do the Comet aircraft failures teach us', https://www.engineersireland.ie/Engineers-Journal/Mechanical/beyond-the-limits-of-imagination-what-do-the-comet-aircraft-failures-teach-us

c3.text: On 10 January 1954 Comet G-ALYP broke up in flight off Elba; all 35 aboard died.

c4.text: On 8 April 1954 Comet G-ALYY broke up in flight over the sea near Naples; the Comets were grounded again.

c5.text: Wreckage of G-ALYP was salvaged from the sea off Elba; by the end of August 1954 about 70 % had been recovered.
sources: Wikipedia, 'de Havilland Comet', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Comet (70 per cent by weight of the main structure)

c6.text: Investigators tested Comet G-ALYU in a water tank, pressurising it again and again; it failed from metal fatigue after the equivalent of about 3,000 flights.
sources: Engineers Ireland, 'Beyond the limits of imagination: what do the Comet aircraft failures teach us', https://www.engineersireland.ie/Engineers-Journal/Mechanical/beyond-the-limits-of-imagination-what-do-the-comet-aircraft-failures-teach-us

c7.text: The Elba failure was traced to the ADF window, a square cut-out in the roof, not a passenger window; fatigue cracks started around the rivets there.
sources: Wikipedia, 'BOAC Flight 781', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BOAC_Flight_781 ('the forward ADF window in the roof'; cracks 'around the rivet')
Wikipedia, 'de Havilland Comet', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Comet ('square cut-outs for the ADF antennas')

c8.text: A pressurised cabin is loaded on every flight; the stress on the fuselage is proportional to the pressure difference between inside and outside, so airliners keep cabin altitude at or below 8,000 feet rather than sea level.

c9.text: Metal fatigue: loads far below breaking strength, repeated many times, grow small cracks until the part fails.

c10.text: Stress concentrates where the edge of an opening curves most sharply: around a round hole it rises to about three times the surrounding stress, and as a corner's radius goes to zero the peak stress grows without limit.
sources: M. E. Tuttle, University of Washington, 'Stress Concentration' lecture, https://courses.washington.edu/mengr556/StressConcentrationLecture.pdf

c11.text: The Comet returned as the redesigned Comet 4 in 1958, with a thickened fuselage skin.
sources: Wikipedia, 'de Havilland Comet', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Comet (Comet 4 debuted 1958; skin thickened)
Aerossurance, 'Common Comet Misconceptions', https://aerossurance.com/safety-management/comet-misconceptions/ (Comet 4 in commercial service from October 1958)

c12.text: The Comet accidents changed the requirements for airliners: they are designed so that cracks are found and tolerated (fail-safe / damage tolerance) before they can bring the structure down.
sources: Wikipedia, 'de Havilland Comet', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Comet (fail-safe or safe-life standards)

c13.text: A cabin window has three panes; the small hole is in the middle pane, so the outer pane carries the cabin pressure.
sources: Time, 'This Is Why There Are Holes in Airplane Windows', https://time.com/3903109/airplane-window-holes
IFLScience, 'Why Do Airplane Windows Have A Tiny Hole In Them?', https://www.iflscience.com/why-is-there-a-tiny-hole-in-airplane-windows-82433

c14.text: The hole lets moisture out of the gap between the panes, which keeps the window from fogging.
sources: Time, 'This Is Why There Are Holes in Airplane Windows', https://time.com/3903109/airplane-window-holes
IFLScience, 'Why Do Airplane Windows Have A Tiny Hole In Them?', https://www.iflscience.com/why-is-there-a-tiny-hole-in-airplane-windows-82433

scenes.say: Next time you fly, look at the window. Not through it. At it. There is not a single sharp corner anywhere.

image.subject: a modern airliner cabin window seen from the aisle seat
image.show: a rounded oval cabin window with soft corners, a pulled-up shade, a passenger's hand resting on the armrest, blue sky and clouds outside

scenes.motion: clouds drift slowly past outside the oval window; the passenger's fingers tap the armrest once; a gentle cabin vibration

scenes.say: That shape is not style. It is a lesson, and it was learned the hard way.

image.subject: an airliner window seat seen from behind the passenger
image.show: a passenger's silhouette looking out of a rounded oval cabin window at a wing and blue sky, soft cabin light

scenes.motion: the passenger slowly leans toward the window; the wing tip flexes slightly; clouds slide past

scenes.say: In the next few minutes, we will follow that lesson from a quiet cabin in 1954 to the tiny hole in the window beside you.

image.subject: an old 1950s jet cabin turning into a modern cabin
image.show: on the left half a 1950s cabin with a squarish window and a woman in a hat, on the right half a modern cabin with an oval window and a phone on the tray table, split by a soft line

scenes.motion: sunlight sweeps slowly from the old cabin on the left to the modern one on the right; clouds drift past both windows

scenes.say: Your house has square windows. So does your car, your office, your train. Square is easy to cut, easy to frame, easy to fit.

image.subject: a row of ordinary buildings and a city tram
image.show: square house windows, a square office window and a tram with square windows side by side on a sunny street

scenes.motion: the tram rolls slowly along the street; curtains sway in an open square house window; a bird lands on a window sill

scenes.say: A square window is the most natural shape in the world. Builders have made them that way for centuries, and nothing bad happens.

image.subject: a carpenter fitting a square wooden window frame into a brick wall
image.show: a cheerful carpenter in an apron pressing a square wooden window frame into a brick wall, a level tool on the sill

scenes.motion: the carpenter pushes the frame into place and taps it with a mallet; sawdust drifts down

scenes.say: So why does an airliner, one of the most carefully designed machines on Earth, refuse to have a single one?

image.subject: a modern twin-engine airliner parked at a gate
image.show: side view of the fuselage showing a long row of small oval windows, ground crew walking beneath

scenes.motion: a baggage cart drives slowly past under the wing; a ground worker walks along the fuselage; heat shimmer over the apron

scenes.say: To find out, we have to go back to the first jet airliner, and to a crack smaller than your fingernail.

image.subject: a single tiny crack in a sheet of aluminium beside rivets
image.show: an extreme close-up of polished aircraft aluminium with a row of rivets and one hair-thin dark crack starting at a rivet hole, shown in red

scenes.motion: the camera light glints across the metal; the thin red crack lengthens a tiny bit in one short jump

scenes.say: On the second of May, 1952, a de Havilland Comet took off from London for Johannesburg.

image.subject: a 1950s de Havilland Comet 1 jet airliner taking off from a London airfield
image.show: the sleek silver Comet with four jet engines buried in the wing roots and squarish cabin windows climbing away, a small crowd waving behind a fence

scenes.motion: the Comet lifts off and climbs slowly away; the crowd waves hats and handkerchiefs; grass bends in the jet wash

scenes.say: It was the first jet airliner ever to carry paying passengers.

image.subject: passengers in 1950s coats climbing the boarding steps of a silver Comet jet
image.show: excited passengers with hats and handbags walking up mobile steps into the open door of a sleek silver jet airliner, a smiling stewardess at the top, morning light

scenes.motion: passengers climb the steps one by one; the stewardess greets them with a nod; a coat flaps in the breeze

scenes.say: There were stops on the way, but the age of the jet had begun. People who had flown in rattling propeller planes could not believe how smooth it was.

image.subject: the cabin of a 1950s Comet in calm flight
image.show: passengers in 1950s clothes relaxing in wide seats beside nearly square windows, a stewardess pouring tea, a cup of tea on a tray table, sunlight

scenes.motion: the stewardess pours tea slowly into a cup; a passenger leans back and smiles; sunlight moves across the seats

scenes.say: It felt like the future had arrived early. Higher, faster and smoother than anything that had flown passengers before.

image.subject: passengers in a 1950s jet cabin looking out in wonder
image.show: a boy with his face close to a squarish window pointing at clouds below, his mother smiling beside him, quiet cabin

scenes.motion: the boy points and presses closer to the window; his mother leans over to look; clouds drift past below

scenes.say: The Comet was built to cruise at around forty thousand feet, far above the weather.

image.subject: a Comet jet airliner high above the clouds
image.show: the silver Comet, a pure jet with NO propellers, its four jet engines buried inside the wing roots, small against a deep blue sky far above a sea of white clouds

scenes.motion: the Comet glides slowly across the frame; clouds below drift the other way; a thin contrail trails behind

scenes.say: Up there the air is far too thin to breathe. So the cabin is sealed and pumped full of air, like a balloon with people inside.

image.subject: a cutaway of a jet airliner fuselage in flight
image.show: a side cutaway showing seated passengers inside a sealed tube, soft teal arrows of air filling the cabin, thin pale air outside

scenes.motion: teal air arrows flow gently into the cabin and fill it; outside, faint wisps of thin air drift past

scenes.say: Every flight, the fuselage swells a little. Every landing, it relaxes again. One flight, one breath in and out.

image.subject: a balloon-like diagram of a fuselage tube
image.show: the same aircraft tube drawn twice, one slightly swollen with amber outline, one relaxed, a looping arrow between them

scenes.motion: the fuselage tube slowly swells outward, holds, then slowly relaxes, like breathing in and out, twice

scenes.say: Think about what that means for the metal. The air inside pushes outward on every square inch of the skin, the whole time you are up there.

image.subject: air pushing outward on the inside of a fuselage skin
image.show: a close cutaway of a curved aircraft skin panel with many small teal arrows pressing outward from the cabin side, thin pale air outside

scenes.motion: the teal arrows push steadily outward and the curved skin bulges very slightly

scenes.say: Land, open the doors, and the push is gone. Take off again, and it comes back.

image.subject: a 1950s jet parked at a gate with its door open and steps attached
image.show: passengers walking down mobile steps from the open door of a silver jet airliner onto the apron, evening light

scenes.motion: passengers walk slowly down the steps; a ground worker waves; the evening light fades a little

scenes.say: A short hop and a long flight both count as one full cycle.

image.subject: a simple loop diagram of one flight cycle
image.show: a cartoon airliner climbing up one side of a looping arrow and descending the other, with a soft swollen fuselage at the top of the loop and a relaxed one at the bottom

scenes.motion: the small airliner travels once around the looping arrow; the fuselage swells at the top and relaxes at the bottom

scenes.say: That is why modern cabins are not kept at sea level. They are kept at no higher than about eight thousand feet, to go easier on the metal.

image.subject: a cabin pressure gauge in a cockpit panel
image.show: a round analogue cabin altitude gauge with its needle resting in an amber band among other cockpit dials

scenes.motion: the needle rises slowly and settles in the amber band; a small light blinks once

scenes.say: For almost two years, the Comet was the pride of British aviation.

image.subject: a crowd admiring a Comet jet on display at an airfield
image.show: families in 1950s clothes gathered around a gleaming silver Comet jet on a sunny airfield, a child on a father's shoulders

scenes.motion: the child waves a small flag; people point at the jet; flags flutter in the breeze

scenes.say: Then, on the tenth of January, 1954, a Comet climbed away from Rome toward London.

image.subject: a Comet jet airliner climbing over the blue Mediterranean coast
image.show: the silver Comet seen from far away climbing above a calm blue sea and the hills of an island, bright winter afternoon

scenes.motion: the small silver jet climbs slowly across the sky; gentle waves sparkle on the sea far below

scenes.say: Near the island of Elba, witnesses saw something they could not understand.

image.subject: two fishermen in a small wooden boat on a calm sea near a hilly island
image.show: two anonymous fishermen pausing with their net and turning to look up at the empty sky with puzzled faces, the island of Elba behind them, bright winter afternoon

scenes.motion: the boat rocks gently; the fishermen slowly turn their heads up toward the sky; the net drips water

scenes.say: High in the sky, the jet broke apart. All thirty-five people on board were lost.

image.subject: a distant mid-air breakup of a jet airliner seen from a beach far below
image.show: a wide view mostly of empty blue sky and calm sea; far away and high up, a TINY silver jet airliner silhouette, as small as a fingernail in the frame, broken into two separate halves with a few small fragments, each trailing a thin grey smoke line downward; seen only from outside as a distant shape, no interior, no seats, no people, no flash, no fire, no sparks

scenes.motion: the two halves of the jet drift slowly apart and tilt downward, trailing grey smoke; small panels flutter down; the sea below stays calm

scenes.say: No storm. No warning. No call from the crew. Only a trail of smoke, slowly fading over the sea.

image.subject: an empty clear blue sky over a calm sea
image.show: an empty winter sky above a calm sea with a faint thin grey smoke trail slowly fading, no aircraft

scenes.motion: the faint smoke trail slowly thins and fades away; small waves glint on the sea

scenes.say: The Comets were stopped and checked. Nothing obvious was found. After a few changes, they flew again.

image.subject: a hangar with a Comet jet airliner and engineers in 1950s overalls
image.show: engineers on ladders inspecting the wing and engines of a Comet under hangar lights, toolboxes on the floor

scenes.motion: an engineer on a ladder runs a torch slowly along the wing; another writes on a clipboard; hangar lights hum

scenes.say: Investigators had theories, but almost no evidence. Most of the aircraft was lying at the bottom of the sea.

image.subject: investigators studying a few small pieces of debris on a table
image.show: engineers in 1950s suits leaning over a long table with only three small bent metal pieces and a seat cushion, a big empty sea chart on the wall

scenes.motion: an engineer turns a small bent piece over in his hands; another taps the empty sea chart

scenes.say: Then, on the eighth of April, near Naples, it happened again.

image.subject: an empty airport gate in the 1950s
image.show: an empty waiting area with a forgotten suitcase and a hat on a bench, rain on the large window, a departures board in the distance

scenes.motion: rain runs down the window; a light above the gate flickers once; the hat on the bench stays still

scenes.say: Two of the most modern airliners in the world had simply come apart in clear sky. The whole Comet fleet was grounded.

image.subject: a row of grounded Comet jet airliners parked on a grey airfield
image.show: several silver Comets parked in a line with covers on their engines under a grey sky, no people

scenes.motion: grey clouds drift slowly overhead; a canvas engine cover flaps gently in the wind

scenes.say: Now nobody could fly the Comet. The pride of British aviation was sitting on the ground, and no one could say exactly why.

image.subject: a newspaper on a café table about the grounded Comet
image.show: a 1950s café table with a folded newspaper showing a drawing of a jet airliner, a coffee cup, rain on the window

scenes.motion: steam rises from the coffee; rain runs down the window; the newspaper page lifts slightly in a draught

scenes.say: Investigators needed the wreckage. Off Elba, ships hunted for pieces on the seabed, with divers and grabs.

image.subject: a 1950s salvage ship on the sea lowering a grab
image.show: a grey salvage ship with a crane lowering a metal grab into the water, a diver's boat alongside, calm sea

scenes.motion: the crane slowly lowers the grab into the water; the ship rocks gently; ripples spread

scenes.say: By the end of that summer, about seventy percent of the aircraft had been brought up and laid out, piece by piece, on a frame.

image.subject: aircraft wreckage being reassembled on a wooden frame in a hangar
image.show: bent silver panels of a jet fuselage fixed to a large wooden frame, engineers in coats studying them

scenes.motion: an engineer lifts a bent panel into place on the frame; another steps back to look; dust drifts in a light beam

scenes.say: Every twisted panel was a clue. But the panels alone could not say what had torn them apart.

image.subject: a twisted, torn panel of aircraft skin on a workbench
image.show: a crumpled silver fuselage panel with torn rivet lines lying on a wooden bench under a lamp, a ruler beside it

scenes.motion: the lamp swings slightly and its light moves over the torn edges; dust drifts in the beam

scenes.say: At the same time, engineers did something astonishing. They took a whole Comet and put it in a giant tank of water.

image.subject: a complete Comet jet fuselage sitting inside a huge water tank
image.show: a silver Comet fuselage with wings sticking out of a long concrete tank filled with water, engineers on a walkway above

scenes.motion: the water ripples gently around the fuselage; an engineer walks slowly along the walkway; pipes vibrate

scenes.say: Water was pumped into the cabin and let out again, over and over. Each pump was one flight.

image.subject: a cutaway diagram of an EMPTY test fuselage inside a water tank being pressurised
image.show: an empty aircraft fuselage with no seats and no people inside, sitting in a concrete water tank, teal water arrows pumped into the empty cabin and drained out in a loop, a pump and pressure gauge beside the tank

scenes.motion: the water level inside the empty cabin rises, then falls, then rises again; the gauge needle swings up and back

scenes.say: And water, unlike air, would not explode if the cabin burst.

image.subject: a comparison of a bursting air balloon and a gently leaking water balloon
image.show: on the left a balloon bursting with a sharp pop of air lines, on the right a water-filled balloon with a small split letting water trickle out calmly, simple cartoon

scenes.motion: the air balloon on the left bursts outward; the water balloon on the right splits and water trickles out gently

scenes.say: After the equivalent of about three thousand flights, the cabin split open.

image.subject: a split in the side of a fuselage inside a water tank
image.show: close view of a Comet fuselage in a water tank with a long tear opening in its upper skin and a rush of bubbles escaping

scenes.motion: the tear in the skin widens a little and a rush of bubbles pours out into the tank water

scenes.say: That test changed how the world thinks about aircraft. Not how strong a cabin is on its first flight, but how strong it still is on its thousandth.

image.subject: a 1950s engineer at a chalkboard next to a scale model of a jet
image.show: an engineer chalking a simple line graph that falls over many flights, a small model jet airliner on the desk, a colleague watching

scenes.motion: the engineer draws the falling line on the chalkboard; chalk dust drifts; the colleague nods slowly

scenes.say: Day and night, the pumps worked. It was like flying the same aircraft over and over, without ever leaving the ground.

image.subject: engineers watching a pressure test control panel at night
image.show: two engineers in a dim 1950s control room watching a wall of gauges and a counter, a clock showing late night, a thermos on the desk

scenes.motion: the counter clicks up; a gauge needle swings up and back; one engineer pours coffee from the thermos

scenes.say: Three thousand flights. Not a storm, not a bomb. Just the cabin breathing in and out, again and again.

image.subject: a paperclip being bent back and forth by two fingers
image.show: close-up of two fingers bending a steel paperclip back and forth, a tiny red crack appearing at the bend

scenes.motion: the fingers bend the paperclip back and forth slowly; on the fourth bend a tiny red crack appears at the bend

scenes.say: The name for that is metal fatigue.

image.subject: a magnified view of a tiny crack growing in metal grains
image.show: a close-up of grey metal grains with a thin red crack creeping between them, a magnifying lens edge framing it

scenes.motion: the red crack creeps forward between the metal grains in tiny steps

scenes.say: Bend a paperclip once, nothing happens. Bend it again and again and it snaps, though you never pushed hard.

image.subject: a broken paperclip in a palm
image.show: an open palm holding a steel paperclip snapped into two pieces at its bend

scenes.motion: the hand stays still; soft window light slowly moves across the palm and the two broken paperclip pieces; one small piece rocks very slightly

scenes.say: Small loads, repeated, grow tiny cracks.

image.subject: a row of small identical arrows hitting a metal bar
image.show: many small identical teal arrows tapping one after another on a metal bar, a tiny red crack forming where they hit

scenes.motion: small teal arrows tap the bar one after another; a tiny red crack slowly appears and grows

scenes.say: The tank had answered one question: what broke the Comet. Now the wreck had to answer a second one: where exactly did it begin?

image.subject: the rebuilt wreckage on its frame seen from a distance
image.show: a long hangar with the reassembled Comet wreckage on a wooden frame, a single engineer standing in front of it with a clipboard

scenes.motion: the engineer slowly walks along the frame looking up; light shafts from high windows drift

scenes.say: The scary part is that you cannot see it coming. The crack is tiny for most of its life. Then, all at once, it is not.

image.subject: a hair-thin crack hidden in aircraft skin
image.show: an extreme close-up of riveted aluminium skin where a nearly invisible thin crack shows only under a magnifying glass edge

scenes.motion: the magnifying glass slides over the metal and the thin crack comes into view

scenes.say: But a crack has to start somewhere. And on the rebuilt wreck from Elba, the investigators found where.

image.subject: an engineer with a magnifying glass studying a bent piece of aircraft roof
image.show: an engineer in a 1950s suit leaning close with a magnifying glass over a torn panel with a squarish opening

scenes.motion: the engineer slowly moves the magnifying glass along the panel and stops; his eyebrows rise

scenes.say: It was not a passenger window. It was a small, squarish opening in the roof, for a radio navigation antenna.

image.subject: the roof of a Comet fuselage seen from above
image.show: the top of the silver fuselage with two small squarish cut-outs near the front, one marked in red

scenes.motion: the camera drifts slowly over the roof; the red outline of one squarish opening glows softly

scenes.say: Around the rivets at its edge, a fatigue crack had grown, flight after flight, until the roof tore open.

image.subject: a close-up of the corner of a squarish cut-out in aircraft skin
image.show: rivets around a sharp square corner, a red crack running from a rivet hole at the corner outward

scenes.motion: the red crack grows outward from the rivet hole in short jumps

scenes.say: So the famous story, square passenger windows broke the Comet, is not quite right. But the reason it broke is exactly why your window is round.

image.subject: a modern oval airliner window next to a crossed-out square window
image.show: a rounded oval airplane window on the left and a square window outline on the right with a red diagonal cross over it

scenes.motion: the red cross draws itself slowly over the square window; the oval window glows softly

scenes.say: Here is why. Think of the force in the skin as water flowing in a river.

image.subject: a calm river flowing evenly
image.show: smooth parallel streams of teal water flowing straight across the frame

scenes.motion: the teal water flows smoothly and evenly from left to right

scenes.say: Put a rock in the river. The water has to go around it, and it speeds up at the sides.

image.subject: water flowing around a round rock in a river
image.show: teal flow lines bending smoothly around a round grey rock, the lines bunched slightly at its sides in amber

scenes.motion: the water flows around the rock; small swirls form at its sides and drift away

scenes.say: A hole in metal works the same way. The stress flows around it. Even a perfect circle makes it about three times stronger at the edges.

image.subject: a flat metal plate with a round hole being pulled from both sides
image.show: teal stress lines flowing around a circular hole, amber where they crowd at the top and bottom of the hole, arrows pulling the plate

scenes.motion: the arrows pull gently; the stress lines flow around the hole and the amber glow pulses at its edges

scenes.say: Now make the hole square. The lines cannot bend gently around a sharp corner. They pile up into it.

image.subject: a flat metal plate with a square hole being pulled from both sides
image.show: teal stress lines crowding tightly into the four sharp corners of a square hole, the corners glowing red

scenes.motion: the stress lines squeeze into the corners; the red glow at each corner grows brighter and brighter

scenes.say: The sharper the corner, the higher the stress at its tip. In theory, at a perfectly sharp corner, there is no limit at all.

image.subject: a sharp corner tip under a magnifier with glowing stress
image.show: a magnified sharp corner of a cut-out with stress lines converging into its tip, the tip glowing bright red

scenes.motion: the stress lines squeeze tighter into the tip and its red glow brightens step by step

scenes.say: Add rivet holes close to that corner, and you have tiny weak spots sitting near the most stressed point of the opening.

image.subject: a square corner with a rivet hole at its tip in a stress diagram
image.show: the red glowing corner of a square opening with one rivet hole right at the tip, a tiny red crack starting from it

scenes.motion: the red glow pulses at the corner; a tiny crack creeps out from the rivet hole in one short jump

scenes.say: This is not only true of aircraft. Wherever metal is loaded again and again,

image.subject: a steel crane base and a machine bracket with rounded inside corners
image.show: a construction crane's steel base plate and a machine bracket side by side, every inside corner smoothly rounded and outlined in amber

scenes.motion: the crane arm slowly swings above; amber outlines trace around the rounded corners

scenes.say: in cranes, brackets and engines, engineers round the inside corners.

image.subject: an engine part with smoothly rounded inside corners
image.show: a close-up of a shiny machined engine bracket whose inside corners are smoothly rounded, outlined in soft amber, on a workshop bench

scenes.motion: a workshop lamp light glides slowly over the bracket; the amber outlines on the rounded corners glow softly

scenes.say: Engineers call this a stress concentration. And they have learned to fear sharp corners.

image.subject: an engineering drawing comparing sharp and rounded corners
image.show: a blueprint-style drawing of a sharp-cornered notch glowing red beside a rounded notch glowing soft amber, an engineer's pencil resting on it

scenes.motion: the pencil slowly traces the rounded corner; the red glow on the sharp notch pulses

scenes.say: Now repeat that every flight. The cabin breathes in, the corner is pulled hard. It breathes out. In, out. Thousands of times.

image.subject: a fuselage cabin breathing in and out with a stressed corner
image.show: a fuselage tube drawn with one square opening whose corner flashes red each time the tube swells

scenes.motion: the tube swells and relaxes in a slow rhythm and the corner flashes red each time it swells

scenes.say: Round off the corner, and the lines can bend smoothly around it. The load is spread out. The peak stress drops.

image.subject: a metal plate with an oval rounded window opening
image.show: teal stress lines flowing smoothly around an oval opening with only a soft amber glow at its sides

scenes.motion: the stress lines flow calmly around the oval; the soft amber glow stays gentle

scenes.say: That is the whole secret. Not stronger glass, and not thicker metal. Just a curve.

image.subject: a single smooth curve drawn on paper
image.show: an engineer's hand drawing a single smooth rounded corner with a compass on cream paper

scenes.motion: the compass turns slowly and draws the smooth curve

scenes.say: The Comet came back in 1958 as the Comet 4, redesigned, with a thicker skin, built on what the tank had taught.

image.subject: a de Havilland Comet 4 jet airliner flying
image.show: the longer silver Comet 4 with a row of oval windows flying over green countryside in bright sun

scenes.motion: the Comet 4 flies slowly across the frame; its shadow slides over the fields below

scenes.say: Look closely at the windows on any airliner today, and at its doors and hatches. Every corner is rounded.

image.subject: a modern airliner door and cargo hatch with rounded corners
image.show: close side view of a modern airliner's passenger door and a cargo hatch, both with clearly rounded corners, ground crew below

scenes.motion: a ground worker walks past under the door; a baggage belt moves slowly toward the hatch

scenes.say: Today, airliners are inspected for cracks on a schedule, long before any of them can grow large.

image.subject: an engineer inspecting a modern airliner fuselage with a handheld device
image.show: an engineer in a hi-vis vest on a platform holding a small inspection probe against the fuselage skin around a window, hangar lights

scenes.motion: the engineer slides the probe slowly along the skin; a small screen on the device shows a moving line

scenes.say: But the real change was bigger than one aircraft.

image.subject: a modern fuselage fatigue test rig
image.show: a large airliner fuselage section held in a steel test frame with hydraulic jacks and cables, engineers watching screens

scenes.motion: hydraulic jacks push gently and release in rhythm; a screen line ticks upward; an engineer leans toward a monitor

scenes.say: After the Comet, the rules changed. Fatigue became something every airliner is designed and tested against.

image.subject: engineers watching a modern fatigue test counter in a control room
image.show: two engineers in a control room watching a large screen with a counter of simulated flights ticking upward next to a live view of a fuselage in a test rig

scenes.motion: the flight counter ticks upward; one engineer points at the screen; the other nods

scenes.say: Structures are built so that a crack is found before it can run. If one part fails, the cabin is meant to hold together.

image.subject: the inside of an airliner fuselage skin with frames and straps
image.show: a cutaway of curved aircraft skin with ribs, stringers and a metal strap across them, a small red crack stopping right at the strap

scenes.motion: a small red crack creeps toward the strap and stops at it

scenes.say: And there is one more detail in your window, if you look closely. A tiny hole, near the bottom.

image.subject: a close-up of an airliner window
image.show: a rounded cabin window with a tiny hole visible in the plastic pane near the bottom, clouds beyond

scenes.motion: clouds drift past outside; the light shifts softly on the plastic pane around the tiny hole

scenes.say: A cabin window has three panes. The tiny hole is in the middle one. So the outer pane carries the cabin pressure.

image.subject: a cutaway of an airliner window showing three panes
image.show: three curved window panes stacked in a frame, the middle pane with a tiny hole, teal arrows showing air passing through it, the outer pane outlined in amber

scenes.motion: a teal air arrow passes slowly through the tiny hole in the middle pane; the outer pane glows softly amber

scenes.say: The same little hole also lets moist air out of the gap, so the window does not fog up on a long flight.

image.subject: a window gap between panes fogging and clearing
image.show: a close cutaway of the gap between two window panes with tiny droplets drifting out through a small hole, the pane turning clear

scenes.motion: tiny droplets drift slowly out through the small hole and the misted pane clears

scenes.say: Three panes, one tiny hole, and four rounded corners. Everything about that small window was shaped by what engineers learned from the Comet.

image.subject: a cabin window with three panes, a tiny hole and four rounded corners
image.show: a front view of a rounded airliner window with its frame, three thin outlines of panes and a tiny hole, sunset clouds outside

scenes.motion: sunset light shifts slowly across the window; clouds drift past outside

scenes.say: So next time you sit by a window, look at that shape again. That curve is a lesson written into the metal.

image.subject: a young traveller at a window seat touching the window frame
image.show: a young traveller with headphones around the neck gently tracing the rounded corner of the window with a finger, wing and sky outside

scenes.motion: the finger slowly traces the rounded corner; the traveller smiles; clouds drift past

scenes.say: Thousands of flights a day, cabins breathing in and out, and not one sharp corner to catch the load.

image.subject: a modern airliner climbing at sunset
image.show: an airliner with a row of oval windows climbing into a golden sunset over a city, lights coming on below

scenes.motion: the airliner climbs slowly into the golden sky; city lights twinkle on below

scenes.say: Nothing is ordinary, once you know how it really works.

image.subject: an airliner window glowing at night above city lights
image.show: a row of glowing oval airliner windows seen from outside at night, city lights far below

scenes.motion: the airliner glides slowly past; the window lights glow warmly; city lights twinkle below
